newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemalans decry loss of U.N. human rights expert.
newsitem.headline: Guatemalans decry loss of U.N. human rights expert.

text.p: Human rights and religious leaders on Wednesday decried a United Nations decision to stop sending an independent expert to Guatemala to investigate human rights violations.
"The U.N.'s decision ... will mean a lack of accountability during a key time," Carlos Aldana, spokesman for the Guatemalan archbishop's office, told Reuters.

Aldana and human rights leaders said it was important for the United Nations to keep a close eye on human rights this year because abuses continued despite Guatemala having been at peace for three months after 36 years of civil war.

The government and leftist rebels signed a historic peace treaty on Dec. 29, ending a war that earned the Guatemalan army a reputation for wholesale violations of human rights, including torture and massacres of civilians.

Since 1987, the United Nations has sent an independent human rights expert to Guatemala. For the past four years, Argentine Monica Pinto has been assigned to the country and her reports have indicated slow but steady improvements in human rights.
On Wednesday, the United Nations Human Rights Commission, which is meeting in Geneva this month, decided to recall Pinto and send an ad hoc commission later this year in her place.
The commission is considered less rigorous than an expert because rather than conducting in-depth investigations and interviews, it would depend on government and other reports.
"The commission will not have the same depth or impact that the independent investigator had," Aldana said.

Amelia Garcia, coordinator for the Mutual Support Group, which works with families of people who have disappeared, acknowledged human rights abuses have declined in the last year, but told Reuters that they continue to occur.
"We are very upset that the position of independent expert will not be extended for at least another year," she said.
The government, however, applauded the United Nation's decision.

"This indicates the international community's confidence in the advances in human rights that have taken place under President Alvaro Arzu," Gabriel Aguilera, deputy foreign relations minister, said in a statement.
